faqs.a: The 50/30/20 rule suggests 50% of income for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings. It is a starting point, not a law; adjust the split to your income and cost of living.

Subtracting total expenses from income gives your surplus. If it is negative, you are spending more than you earn and need to cut expenses or raise income. A savings rate of 20% or more is a strong position.
faqs.q: What is a good savings rate?

faqs.a: Pay yourself first: move a fixed amount to savings the day income arrives, then spend what remains. This calculator shows your surplus so you can set that amount confidently.
faqs.q: How do I actually start saving?

faqs.a: List every fixed monthly cost first, then average variable costs over three months. Common misses are subscriptions, annual bills divided by 12, and small daily purchases that add up.
faqs.q: How do I track expenses accurately?

budget-calculator.formula:
total_expenses = housing + food + transport + utilities + other
surplus = income - total_expenses
savings_rate = surplus / income x 100
annual_surplus = surplus x 12
howTo: Enter your total monthly income after tax.
Enter your monthly spending in each of the five categories.
Read your total expenses, remaining surplus and savings rate.
If the surplus is negative, adjust categories until it turns positive.
Revisit monthly and watch the savings rate trend.
keyFacts: A budget compares what comes in against what goes out each month.
The surplus is income minus expenses; a negative surplus means you are spending more than you earn.
The savings rate is the share of income you keep; 20% or more is considered strong.
Housing is usually the largest expense, so it is the biggest lever for most people.
Budgets fail most often from untracked small purchases, not from big planned costs.

budget-calculator.quickAnswer: With $5,000 monthly income and $3,000 in expenses ($1,500 housing, $600 food, $300 transport, $200 utilities, $400 other), you keep $2,000 per month — a 40% savings rate, or $24,000 per year.
budget-calculator.tagline: See where your money goes and what you keep.
budget-calculator.workedExample:
Income $5,000 per month. Expenses: housing $1,500 + food $600 + transport $300 + utilities $200 + other $400 = $3,000 total.

Surplus = 5,000 - 3,000 = $2,000 per month. Savings rate = 2,000 / 5,000 x 100 = 40%. Annual surplus = 2,000 x 12 = $24,000 per year.
